claims.text: The investigated material consists of sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The initial nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral shapes.
In sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt particles, surface-energy minimization dominates configurational-entropy stabilization.
For nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm, the surface term γA dominates the total Gibbs free energy.
Reshaping toward a sphere lowers nanoparticle surface area and therefore surface energy.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than Co, Ni, and Pt.
Au and Cu have higher vapor pressures than Co, Ni, and Pt under the relevant heating conditions.
Au and Cu segregate to the nanoparticle surface to reduce the total Gibbs free energy.
Au/Cu surface segregation creates a chemical-potential or concentration gradient that accelerates surface diffusion relative to bulk lattice diffusion.
Short surface-diffusion paths and the large surface-energy driving force overcome the nominal sluggish-diffusion effect in these nanoparticles.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu evaporate during heating, causing nanoparticle shrinkage and loss.
The critical temperature for rapid Au/Cu surface diffusion, shape rounding, and size reduction is approximately 600–700 K.
Above the critical temperature, particle number density progressively decreases because of evaporation.
Above the critical temperature, the particle-size distribution widens through an Ostwald-ripening-like process driven by surface evaporation.
After Au and Cu depletion, the remaining particles become spherical and enriched in Pt, Co, and Ni.
Initially icosahedral nanoparticles transform into truncated octahedra or spheres faster than bulk alloys recrystallize.
The proposed surface-energy-dominated mechanism is valid only for particles smaller than 10 nm.
For bulk alloys or particles larger than 20 nm, entropy stabilization and sluggish diffusion dominate and prevent rapid segregation and evaporation.
The mechanism assumes vacuum or inert conditions in which evaporation is not suppressed by a reactive atmosphere.
Icosahedral and truncated-octahedral starting shapes can have different activation energies for shape change and therefore different onset temperatures.
